seoTitle: Compound Interest Calculator - Calculate Investment Future Value
metaDescription: Free compound interest calculator. Project how your savings and investments grow over time using the power of compounding with regular monthly contributions.
intro: Harness the power of compounding with our free Compound Interest Calculator. Whether you are planning for retirement, building an emergency fund, or investing in the stock market, this tool projects the future value of your savings by combining your initial deposit, regular monthly contributions, and the exponential force of compound interest. See exactly how time and consistent saving can grow your wealth far beyond what you put in.
whatIs: Compound interest is the process by which the interest earned on an investment is reinvested, so that interest earns interest in subsequent periods. It is often described as 'interest on interest,' and it is the fundamental mechanism behind the growth of long-term investments. Unlike simple interest, which is calculated only on the principal amount, compound interest accelerates wealth accumulation by applying interest to an ever-growing base. The more frequently interest is compounded — daily, monthly, quarterly, or annually — the faster your money grows. This calculator lets you model all these scenarios accurately.
howToUse: Enter your Initial Investment amount — the lump sum you are starting with today.
Input any Monthly Contribution you plan to add regularly to your savings.
Set the Annual Interest Rate you expect to earn on your investment.
Specify the number of Years to Grow — the total duration of your investment horizon.
Choose the Compound Frequency (e.g., Annually, Quarterly, Monthly, Daily).
Click 'Calculate Growth' to see your projected future value, total contributions, and total interest earned.
howItWorks: The calculator applies the compound interest formula: A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt), where A is the future value, P is the principal, r is the annual interest rate (in decimal), n is the number of times interest compounds per year, and t is the time in years. For regular monthly contributions, it uses the future value of an annuity formula alongside the lump-sum formula and sums both values to produce the complete projected balance. The difference between your total contributions and the projected balance represents the total interest earned through compounding.
workedExample: If you start with $5,000 as your initial deposit, add $200 every month, and earn a 7% annual interest rate compounded monthly for 10 years: your total contributions will be $29,000 ($5,000 initial + $200 × 120 months). Thanks to compounding, your projected balance at the end of 10 years will be approximately $44,792. This means compounding generated roughly $15,792 in additional wealth — money you earned without any extra effort.
resultInterpretation: The result shows three key figures. Future Value is the total projected balance at the end of your chosen period. Total Invested is the actual cash you deposited (principal plus all contributions). Total Interest Earned is the difference — the wealth generated purely through the compounding effect. A longer time horizon dramatically increases the interest-to-contribution ratio, illustrating why starting to invest early is one of the most powerful personal finance strategies available.
useCases: Retirement Planning: Estimating how much your 401(k), IRA, or pension fund will grow over decades of regular contributions.
Education Savings: Projecting a college savings fund to see if monthly deposits will cover future tuition costs.
Emergency Fund Growth: Seeing how a high-yield savings account compounds over one to five years.
Investment Comparison: Comparing different interest rates or compounding frequencies to make smarter deposit decisions.
Mortgage Overpayments: Understanding how extra principal payments reduce total interest on a home loan.
tipsAndLimitations: Start early: due to the exponential nature of compounding, starting 10 years earlier can more than double your final balance.

This calculator assumes a constant interest rate throughout the entire period, which is rarely the case for stock market investments.
It does not account for inflation, income taxes on interest earned, or investment management fees, all of which reduce real returns.
Compounding frequency matters: daily compounding yields slightly more than monthly, which yields more than annual — though the difference narrows at lower interest rates.

faq.question: What is the difference between compound interest and simple interest?
faq.answer: Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal. Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus all previously accumulated interest. Over long periods, compound interest produces dramatically higher returns.

faq.question: What is the Rule of 72?
faq.answer: The Rule of 72 is a mental math shortcut. Divide 72 by your annual interest rate to estimate how many years it will take to double your money. For example, at 6% annual interest, 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years to double.

faq.question: Does compounding frequency significantly affect my results?
faq.answer: Yes, but the impact depends on the interest rate. At higher rates, more frequent compounding (daily vs. annually) can meaningfully increase your total. At lower rates, the difference is smaller but still present.

faq.question: Can I use this calculator for savings accounts?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Enter the savings account's APY as the annual interest rate, choose monthly compounding, and add your regular monthly deposit to see an accurate projection.
